title: Dacono Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Dacono wells have a 36-foot median depth, but some reach 1,040 feet. See yields, water levels, costs and risks before buying.
h1: Dacono, Colorado Well Depth, Yield and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Dacono means looking past the presence of a well. The local permit records show a wide range of conditions: the median reported depth is 36 feet, while the deepest recorded well reaches 1,040 feet. Reported yields are generally useful, but the records are not complete for every well.

This page covers permitted wells within 5 miles of Dacono in Weld County, including nearby Frederick, Erie, Firestone, Todd Creek, Fort Lupton and Leyner. Use the statistics as a screening tool, then confirm the specific well, permit, pump equipment, water quality and septic limitations on the property you are considering.

sections.heading: Dacono well depths vary sharply across the plains
sections.html:
Dacono’s reported well depth has a median of 36 feet, with the middle half between 18 and 550 feet. That is an unusually broad spread for estimating a new well. Most recorded wells, 61%, are under 100 feet, but 23% are 600 feet or deeper. The 90th-percentile depth is 746 feet, and the deepest record is 1,040 feet.

For a driller’s bid, do not treat the 36-foot median as a guaranteed target. The local ground is Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, and the permit records also name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, Laramie Fox Hills and alluvial water. A nearby well can help establish a starting expectation, but the lot’s geology and the intended aquifer may produce a very different depth.

sections.heading: Most Dacono wells report moderate to strong yield
sections.html:
Only 246 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics describe a subset rather than every permitted well. Among those reports, the median is 10.8 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 9.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-one percent report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 26% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

No reported wells fall under 1 gallon per minute in this dataset, while 3% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. That is encouraging for ordinary household use, but a production rate is not the same as storage in the well or guaranteed long-term supply. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information and any operating limitations before relying on the number.

sections.heading: Dacono water levels look different by measurement period
sections.html:
The median static water level is 15 feet below the surface, but the middle half ranges from 8 to 266 feet. That spread matters when planning a pump, pressure system, trenching and electrical work. A shallow water level does not by itself prove that a well will produce enough water.

The decade series does not show a simple dropping water table in these records. The median measured depth to water was 252 feet in the 1970s, 18 feet in the 2010s and 12 feet in the 2020s. Those figures come from different wells and measurement records, so they should not be read as a continuous trend at one location. Have the current well measured and compare it with its original construction report.

sections.heading: Dacono permit history shows continuing well activity
sections.html:
The Dacono-area records contain 1,915 permitted wells, with 1,016 recorded as constructed. The newest permit year is 2026. Permit activity was 23 in the 1950s, 24 in the 1960s, 122 in the 1970s, 104 in the 1980s, 308 in the 1990s, 295 in the 2000s, 225 in the 2010s and 448 in the 2020s.

Authorized (Pe, Pg) appears most often in the records, with 645 wells. John’s Drilling Inc. (John, Lloyd) appears on 61, and Waneka & Son Drilling (Waneka, Don) on 59. These names describe permit-record activity, not a recommendation or proof that a company is available for your project. Check the current permit status and construction details through Colorado DWR before closing.

sections.heading: What a new Dacono well may cost
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 36-foot median depth, the drilled hole models to about $1,800 to $2,500. That is only the hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $7,800 to $14,500 at the median depth. The depth range in the records explains why a quote can move well beyond that example: 23% of wells are 600 feet or deeper. Get the bid in writing and ask what casing, grout, pump size, pressure equipment, electrical work, access and testing are included.

sections.heading: Dacono buyers need to check water, septic and site risks
sections.html:
The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 1,262 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 37 historic mine features and 9 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped locations do not prove contamination at a particular property, but they are a reason to test the well water and review nearby land uses before purchase. Test for the contaminants appropriate to the property’s setting, not only taste and clarity.

Low yield, an incomplete permit record, a dry hole or an aging pump can change the economics of a rural property. Septic soil conditions, well-to-septic separation, access for a rig and space for tanks or trenching also affect what can be built. Confirm the DWR permit, well construction report, water-rights requirements and county building and septic rules. Exempt household-use wells have limits, including the 35-gpm pumping limit, and some over-appropriated basins require augmentation plans.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Dacono, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Dacono is 36 feet. The middle half runs from 18 to 550 feet, 61% are under 100 feet, and 23% are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest record is 1,040 feet, so a nearby shallow well does not guarantee a shallow drilling plan for your lot.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Dacono?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 36-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $1,800 to $2,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $7,800 to $14,500 at that depth. Deeper drilling can raise the total substantially.

faq.q: How much water do Dacono wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 246 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 10.8 gallons per minute and the middle half is 9.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-one percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute. These figures are not a guarantee for an individual well, so review its pump test and construction report.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Dacono?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that a specific Dacono well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapping shows 1,262 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 37 historic mine features and 9 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property’s water and review nearby environmental records before using it for drinking or cooking.

faq.q: Will a Dacono well work for a new home?
faq.a: The area records show a median yield of 10.8 gallons per minute among reported tests, but only 246 wells report yield. Before building, verify the permit, water-rights requirements, well construction, pump capacity, septic suitability and access for drilling or replacement. Exempt household-use wells also have limits, including the 35-gpm pumping limit.
